sentences.text: Natovenator was a tiny theropod dinosaur that lived in Mongolia during the Late Cretaceous. Its name translates to "swimming hunter" in Latin, while its specific name means "many-toothed" in Greek. This small animal looked remarkably similar to modern waterfowl in its overall appearance.

Gregory S. Paul estimated this creature measured just 0.7 meters in length and weighed only 0.3 kilograms. It possessed a unique set of anatomical traits, including thirteen large, incisiviform teeth in the upper jaw, an hourglass-shaped second metacarpal, and an elongated internarial process on the premaxilla.
The presence of thirteen large, incisiviform premaxillary teeth is a striking feature that distinguishes this species from other small theropods.
The structure of the vertebrae in Natovenator closely resembles that of extinct toothed diving birds known as Hesperornithiformes.

The holotype specimen, cataloged as MPC-D 102/114, was found in the Barun Goyot Formation within Omnogovi Province. This species was formally named Natovenator polydontus in 2022 by a research team led by Sungjin Lee, Yuong-Nam Lee, and Philip J. Currie.
Currently, there is only one recorded fossil occurrence of this dinosaur known to science.

Scientists believe Natovenator was an efficient swimmer adapted to a semiaquatic lifestyle. Its body featured a streamlined dorsal rib cage with ribs oriented toward the rear, a shape also seen in efficient diving birds and mosasaurs. Although the precise mechanics of its swimming are unclear, researchers suggest it used its forelimbs as flippers to propel itself through the water.
Like many modern diving birds, this dinosaur possessed a fairly long neck, a trait likely useful for catching prey underwater.
The research team proposed that a delayed pattern of tooth development might have allowed Natovenator to continue growing enlarged teeth, a phenomenon similar to that observed in sauropterygians.
Phylogenetic analyses place Natovenator as a derived member of the subfamily Halszkaraptorinae within the family Dromaeosauridae.

Fossils of this animal come from the Upper Cretaceous Barun Goyot Formation in Mongolia, dating to approximately 72 million years ago during the Maastrichtian stage. The formation represents a desert environment similar to the current landscape, though the region was slightly wetter during the Mesozoic era.
